summary: Details the schema and protocol elements for representing named subordinate references in LDAP directories. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory can point to another directory for part of its list. This is how those pointers are set up.

questions: what is an ldap referral object
what is the manage dsa it control
what is the ldap ref attribute
how do ldap servers refer to other servers
subtitle: How an LDAP server stores pointers to subtrees that live on other servers, and turns them into referrals.

tldr.problem: An LDAP directory may be spread over several servers, but a server needs a standard way to record that part of the name space is held elsewhere and to tell clients where to go.
tldr.mechanism: A special entry of the referral object class holds one or more URIs in its ref attribute; the server turns them into referrals and search references, and a ManageDsaIT control lets clients treat such entries as ordinary entries.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard that covers named subordinate references only; replication and chaining of operations are explicitly left out.

today: RFC 3296 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers named subordinate references only, leaving other forms of knowledge information to later documents.

sections.title: Why Subordinate References Are Needed
sections.content:
As interest in LDAP directories grew beyond acting as front ends to X.500 directories, there was a need to represent knowledge information more generally. Knowledge information is information about one or more servers, kept in another server, and used to link servers and services together.

This RFC defines schema and protocol elements for named subordinate references. A referral object holds the reference in the directory. It carries one or more URIs in values of the ref attribute, and the server uses them to generate protocol referrals and continuations. The protocol syntax and semantics themselves are defined in RFC 2251.

Other forms of knowledge information are not covered. The RFC also does not describe using subordinate references for replicated environments, or for distributed operations such as chaining an operation from one server to others.
sections.plainLanguage: When one server does not keep part of the list, it can keep a note saying which other server does. This document says how to write and use those notes.

sections.title: The referral Class and the ref Attribute
sections.content:
A referral object is a directory entry whose structural object class is, or is derived from, the referral object class. Its only required attribute is ref. The class SHOULD be used together with the extensibleObject class so the entry can carry the naming attributes used in its Distinguished Name. Referral objects are normally created immediately below object entries within a naming context held by the server.

The ref attribute is multi-valued, case sensitive and has directoryString syntax. Each value MUST follow the labeledURI format of RFC 2079: a URI, optionally followed by whitespace and a label. This RFC does not use the label. If the URI points to an LDAP server, it MUST be an LDAP URL as in RFC 2255. That URL SHOULD NOT contain an explicit scope, filter, attribute list or extensions, and SHOULD contain a non-empty DN.

Servers SHOULD NOT validate the referential integrity of the URI. When building a referral, the server MUST NOT return the separator or label parts of a value, only the URI. The ref value SHOULD NOT be used as a relative name component of an entry's DN.
sections.plainLanguage: A referral entry is a signpost. It has one required field, a list of addresses, and the server only ever hands out the address part and leaves off any extra label.

sections.title: The ManageDsaIT Control
sections.content:
Normally the entries in a referral object are invisible to clients, because the server uses them to build referrals instead. That makes them impossible to edit with ordinary operations. The ManageDsaIT control solves this. Its name is meant to be analogous to the ManageDsaIT service option of X.511(97).

A client MAY attach the control to an add, compare, delete, modify, modifyDN or search request, or to an extended operation that defines it. The control type is 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.2. Its criticality may be TRUE or, if FALSE, absent, and it has no value.

When the control is present, the server SHALL NOT generate a referral or continuation reference from referral objects and SHALL treat them as normal entries. It may still return referrals for other reasons. Note that ref is an operational attribute and is only returned in a search entry when requested.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a 'let me see behind the sign' switch. With it on, you can look at and change the signposts themselves instead of being sent along them.

sections.title: Building a Named Subordinate Reference
sections.content:
To build a reference, create a referral object in the referencing server and give it ref values that point to the matching subtree on the referenced server. Usually the referral object has the same name as the referenced object, which is a context prefix, so the DN of the referral object and the DN of the object on the other server are typically the same.

The RFC's example: server A holds DC=example,DC=net and server B holds DC=sub,DC=example,DC=net. Server A can then hold a referral object named DC=sub,DC=example,DC=net whose ref is ldap://B/DC=sub,DC=example,DC=net.

If ref has several values, the DNs in the LDAP URLs SHOULD be equivalent, and administrators SHOULD avoid configuring naming loops using referrals.
sections.plainLanguage: Server A keeps a card with the same name as the part server B holds, and the card says where to find server B.

sections.title: Referral Handling for Operations
sections.content:
The RFC splits a search into two phases: finding the base object, then doing the search. For both non-search operations (add, compare, delete, modify, modify DN) and for finding a search base, it describes four cases. (1) The object is outside every naming context of the server, so the request is processed as for a non-existent object, or a superior reference is used. (2) The object is itself a referral object, so the server SHOULD return the URIs from its ref values. (3) The object is not held, and the nearest naming context has no referral object above it, so the server generally returns noSuchObject. (4) The object is not held but lies below a referral object, so the server SHOULD return a referral built from that object's URIs.

In every referral, the DN part MUST be changed so it names the right target on the other server. For non-search operations the server SHOULD trim any scope, filter or attribute list from an LDAP URL, but MUST NOT trim critical extensions. For a search base, the server MUST instead put an explicit scope in the URL: base, one or sub, matching the request.

Other operations: a bind SHOULD NOT produce a referral result if the bind name is or is below a referral object. For modify DN, if the new superior is or is below a referral object, the server SHOULD return affectsMultipleDSAs, and also if the new RDN already exists as a referral object, instead of entryAlreadyExists.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask about something that is on a signpost, the server points you to the other server and adjusts the address so it names exactly what you asked for.

sections.title: Worked Examples and Search Continuations
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, server hosta holds O=MNN,C=WW and CN=Manager,O=MNN,C=WW, plus two referral objects. OU=People,O=MNN,C=WW points to hostb and hostc, for example a master and a shadow. OU=Roles,O=MNN,C=WW points to hostd.

A modify request for OU=People,O=MNN,c=WW returns a referral listing both hosts. An add for CN=Manager,OU=Roles,O=MNN,C=WW returns ldap://hostd/CN=Manager,OU=Roles,O=MNN,C=WW. A subtree search whose base is OU=Roles,O=MNN,C=WW returns a referral ending in ??sub.

Once a search base is found and is not a referral object, the search proceeds. For each referral object within scope, regardless of the filter, the server SHOULD return a SearchResultReference built from the URIs of its ref values. A non-LDAP URI is returned as is. An LDAP URL with an absent or empty DN gets the referral object's DN, and an LDAP URL SHOULD get an explicit scope. In a one-level search the added scope is base. Search references may come back in any order.
sections.plainLanguage: When you search a whole area, the server gives you the matching items it has, plus a note for each signpost in the area saying where to search next.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The mechanisms in this RFC can tie LDAP and other servers together. The information that links services together should be protected from unauthorized modification. If the server topology is not public, it should also be protected from unauthorized disclosure.
sections.plainLanguage: The signposts decide where people get sent, so only the right people should be allowed to change them or read them if they are secret.
